analysis.one_liner: Bars health insurers from denying coverage or setting premiums based on genetic information.
analysis.headline: The bill never advanced past subcommittee referral and died when the 104th Congress ended in January 1997, without a vote or a single cosponsor.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would have prohibited health insurers and employer health plans from denying, canceling, or pricing coverage based on a person's genetic information or genetic tests. It would also have stopped insurers from requiring people to take genetic tests or disclose genetic information, and required written permission before any disclosure. Violations could be enforced by state insurance regulators, federal agencies, and private lawsuits.
analysis.who_benefits: People with genetic predispositions to disease, and anyone considering a genetic test, who could otherwise be denied coverage or charged higher premiums based on their DNA. It would also protect family members, since genetic information about blood relatives is covered.
analysis.who_benefits_short: People at genetic risk of disease

how_it_helps.text: Insurers could not deny, cancel, refuse to renew, or vary premiums and terms of coverage based on genetic information or on a request for genetic testing [S3].

Insurers and group health plans could not require anyone to disclose genetic information or obtain a genetic test, and could not disclose genetic information without prior written authorization describing what is disclosed, to whom, and why [S3].

The protections would cover both individual insurers and employer group health plans, enforced through state insurance regulators, federal agencies under ERISA, and a private right of action allowing courts to grant injunctions and monetary damages [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Health insurers and HMOs would bear the cost of new compliance rules and would lose the ability to use genetic information to screen out or price up high-risk customers. If restrictions led people to buy coverage only after learning bad genetic news, insurers argued costs could spread to all premium payers.

drawbacks.text: The bill does not require plans to cover any particular benefit — it only restricts how genetic information is used, so it leaves other coverage rules untouched [S3].

Enforcement for insurers runs through state insurance commissioners, with federal fallback only if a state fails to file or substantially enforce a plan, which could mean uneven protection from state to state [S3].

The bill restricts genetic information specifically, while insurers could still use other medical records to deny or price coverage; critics of such limits have argued that barring risk information can push costs from high-risk individuals onto everyone else through higher premiums.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill offered a clear protection for people with family histories of disease at a moment when genetic testing was expanding, and its disclosure-consent rules were stronger than many later laws. Its main weakness is that it only narrows the slice of information insurers could use, so it addresses genetic discrimination without touching broader underwriting practices, and enforcement would depend heavily on state regulators.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced in August 1996 with no cosponsors, referred to two House committees and then to subcommittees, and no further action was ever taken before the Congress ended.

narrative.text: Rep. Gerald Solomon (R-NY) introduced the bill on August 2, 1996, late in the second session of the 104th Congress [S1].
It was referred to the House Commerce Committee and the Committee on Economic and Educational Opportunities for provisions within their jurisdiction [S5].
On August 12 it was referred to the Commerce Subcommittee on Health and Environment, and on September 6 to the Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee [S5].
No committee marked up the bill, no vote ever occurred, and the 104th Congress ended on January 3, 1997, killing the bill [S1].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Health insurers came out ahead: they kept the ability to collect and use genetic information, and the proposed protections never took effect.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Health insurers kept the status quo

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Health and Environment Subcommittee on August 12, 1996, and took no further action on it

against.what_they_did: Referred the bill to its Employer-Employee Relations Subcommittee on September 6, 1996, and took no further action on it

against.name: House colleagues
against.what_they_did: None joined as cosponsors during the bill's five months of life

sides.party_line_note: The bill had a single Republican sponsor and no cosponsors of either party, so no partisan split on it ever formed in the record.

industries.note: The bill would have barred insurers from denying coverage or setting premiums based on genetic information, barred them from demanding genetic tests or records, and required written consent before disclosing them. Insurers' interest in keeping genetic underwriting tools runs against people with genetic risk, who could face unaffordable or unavailable coverage.

industries.industry: Employers and group health plan sponsors
industries.note: Group health plans would face the same nondiscrimination and disclosure rules, adding compliance duties. Many employers bear premiums for employees, so preventing genetic risk-based pricing also shields workers on company plans.
